stem: You have recently diagnosed a 52-year-old patient with hypothyroidism. She comes to see you to discuss treatment and next steps. Select 3 of the following to discuss with this patient regarding the management of her hypothyroidism:

options.html: You advise her to stop taking lithium because it is exacerbating or causing her hypothyroidism
You recommend that she take levothyroxine to supplement her T4
You warn her about the signs of excessive thyroid hormone supplementation, including sweating, fast heartbeat, tremor, anxiety, and diarrhea
You impress upon her the importance of taking hormone supplementation to reduce the risk of mental retardation
You tell her to increase the dose of all of her other medications by 1.5x to compensate for an expected increase in BMR
You tell her that she will have to repeat blood work so that you can be sure supplementation is adequate

answer:
The correct answers are B, C, F. Management involves replacing thyroid hormone with levothyroxine or liothyronine, or "natural supplement" desiccated thyroid (B). The goal is to titrate to a normal TSH, which requires follow-up blood work (F). Side effects of supplementation are extension effects of the hormone, and patients should be alert to the sympathetic and cardiovascular risks of excess (C).

A is wrong: you should not tell her to stop lithium solely because she has hypothyroidism. E is wrong: do not adjust other drug doses until you know the supplementation is working, at which point it may become necessary. D is wrong: hypothyroidism in adults does not cause mental retardation (that is congenital hypothyroidism), although it may cause decreased mentation and concentration.

stem: Which of the following is untrue regarding RAI uptake and scan?

options.html: A normal test shows 25% of administered iodine is taken up by the thyroid gland
The scan can identify hot nodules, cold nodules, or diffuse pathology
Hot nodules can be identified because they function autonomously from the rest of the gland
The scan is safe for use in pregnancy
Cold nodules are more worrisome for cancer than hot nodules

answer:
The correct answer is D. The scan is contraindicated in pregnancy because it uses radioactive iodine.

The RAI uptake and scan administers 123-I and evaluates uptake (how much iodine enters the gland) then scans the distribution within it. Normally the gland takes up 25% of the administered dose. Distribution should be uniform in a normal test, or in pathology affecting the entire gland such as Graves' or Hashimoto's. Hot nodules are identifiable because they function autonomously - they do not need TSH to drive iodine uptake, whereas the rest of the gland does and therefore takes up nothing (cold gland). Hot nodules are generally not worrisome for cancer; cold nodules are.

stem: A 39-year-old woman comes to your office complaining of a 2-month history of 10lb unintentional weight loss, heat intolerance, and sweating. She is worried that she may be experiencing premature menopause, although her periods continue to be regular. On physical exam, her HR is 88 and pulse is irregular; her RR is 16; her BP is 144/65 sitting; you hear a grade II systolic ejection murmur in the aortic area; her skin is warm and moist; and she has a noticeable stare. On palpation of the thyroid gland, you find that it is slightly large. What is the most likely cause for this patient's presentation?

options.html: She may have premature menopause, but more tests are required to be sure

answer:
The correct answer is B. The question asks for the most likely etiology. All the options are possible, but Graves disease is most likely given the patient's age and sex.

An acute storm would not produce 2 months of symptoms - the same objection applies to post-viral thyroiditis, and she gives no history of a preceding viral infection. Pregnancy is possible but unlikely given continued regular periods. Finally, thyroid disease is more likely than pregnancy given the physical exam findings.

stem: Which of the following is untrue about calcitonin?

options.html: It is a 34 amino acid peptide
It is produced by C cells of the thyroid gland
It is produced by cells of neural developmental origin
It functions in bone by preventing osteoblast activity
It functions in kidney by preventing reabsorption of calcium in the DCT

answer:
The correct answer is D. Calcitonin inhibits osteoclast resorption of bone, not osteoblast activity. It is a hormone of unknown clinical importance, but we do know:

  • Calcitonin is 34 amino acids
  • Produced by C cells (neural origin)
  • Overall function appears to be to decrease circulating calcium
  • Inhibits osteoclast resorption of bone
  • Inhibits calcium resorption at the DCT

stem: \* All of the following would be appropriate treatments for hypercalcemia EXCEPT:
answer: The correct answer is B. This is the only option that would make the hypercalcemia worse, by increasing calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule. (Thiazides block the apical Na/Cl cotransporter, which lowers intracellular Na and thereby drives the basolateral Na/Ca exchanger harder - more calcium into the blood.) IV bisphosphonates and loop diuretics after volume repletion both lower calcium. See 02 - Drugs Affecting Calcium Homeostasis.

stem: Which of the following is not a characteristic of Leydig cells:
answer: The correct answer is B. Leydig cells are located between the seminiferous tubules — it is the Sertoli cells that line the tubule epithelium. Their major function is production of testosterone, via conversion of cholesterol to pregnenolone. LH, secreted by the anterior pituitary, stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone; testosterone in turn exerts negative feedback on hypothalamic GnRH (the stimulus for both LH and FSH). See 11 - Testicular and Ovarian Function.

stem: Which of the following is a physiological effect of androgens in the male.
answer: The correct answer is B. Androgens are crucial for spermatogenesis and differentiation of the male reproductive tract. Non-reproductive effects: muscle anabolism (so A is the wrong direction), proliferation of chondrocytes and eventual closure of the epiphyseal plate (so D is the wrong direction), and activation of sebaceous glands in the skin. Testosterone exerts a negative effect on LH release from the anterior pituitary and on GnRH from the hypothalamus (so C is the wrong direction).

stem: What hormone receptor plays a major role in follicular dominance and atresia?
answer: The correct answer is C. Early in the cycle a surge of estrogen causes negative feedback on FSH, so FSH drops. Follicles without enough FSH receptors cannot respond to the lower hormone level and undergo atresia. The dominant follicle expresses more FSH receptors and keeps responding — this follicle then responds to the LH surge and is ovulated. See 10 - Approach to the Menstrual Cycle.

stem: Fill in the blanks regarding breast tissue development. Estrogen ____________ and progesterone ___________:

options.html: Stimulates fat deposition; stimulates growth of the duct systems
Stimulates growth of the duct systems; promotes lobule development of the mammary glands
Promotes alveoli development of the mammary glands; promotes lobule development of the mammary glands
Promotes lobule development; stimulates fat deposition

answer:
The correct answer is B. estrogen stimulates fat deposition and growth of the duct system of the breast; progesterone promotes development of the lobules and alveoli of the mammary glands.

Note that estrogen does both listed jobs, so A and B each capture half of estrogen's role — B wins because it pairs a true estrogen effect with the correct progesterone effect.

stem: Which cell of the ovary is the primary producer of estradiol, the major female sex steroid?
answer: The correct answer is B. LH stimulates theca interna cells, which produce androgen for aromatization. Aromatization to estrone occurs in the granulosa cells of the follicle when stimulated by FSH. Both processes are cAMP-mediated. Estrone is immediately converted to estradiol. Both theca interna and granulosa cells are part of the follicle, which becomes the corpus luteum.

options.html: Production of small amounts of testosterone

answer:
The correct answer is D. The ovaries produce estrogen and progesterone — regulating the menstrual cycle, pregnancy and secondary sex characteristics — plus small amounts of testosterone.

FSH is produced by the anterior pituitary, not the ovary. FSH acts on the ovary, stimulating growth and development of the ovarian follicles.

stem: Maureen is a 25-year-old female who presents to your clinic complaining of periods that come anywhere from 20-40 days apart and are very unpredictable. This has been a problem since she started her period at the age of 14 and has become very frustrating. She is also concerned about possible fertility problems. She wants to understand what is happening. In your discussions with her which part of her cycle would you focus on as the most likely culprit?
answer:
The correct answer is A. The follicular (proliferative) phase is dominated by FSH and estrogens and involves growth of the primordial follicle to a tertiary follicle, while the uterine lining grows in preparation for implantation. The follicular phase is usually the cause of cycle-length differences between women — for women with irregular cycles, the follicular phase is often the culprit. Problems in this phase can also cause pregnancy loss and infertility.

The ovulatory phase is preceded by the LH surge and is the release of an oocyte. The luteal (secretory) phase is usually fairly consistent between cycles and between women; it is dominated by LH and progesterone, and implantation can occur during it if fertilization has happened.

Boys are taller than girls because they have an accelerated growth rate during puberty

The correct answer is B. No written rationale in the deck; reasoning ours, checked against Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty and Disorders of Puberty.

Boys end up taller because they start later, with their growth spurt at Tanner 3-4 rather than 2-3, not because they grow faster. stem: What statement most accurately describes the hormone abnormalities found in PCOS?

options.html: FSH is constantly overproduced, leading to the development of multiple cystic follicles.
Only androgens produced by the ovaries are found in high concentrations in PCOS; not adrenal sources.
A higher than normal LH surge and LH levels are often found in PCOS.
Most women with PCOS do not yet have any measurable insulin resistance.

answer:
The correct answer is C. In PCOS, LH is relatively overproduced, and LH receptors in thecal and granulosa cells are also overproduced.

A is wrong: FSH is underproduced but at constant levels - the loss of cyclical variation is what forms the cystic follicles. B is wrong: both adrenal and ovarian androgen sources may be overproduced. D is wrong: at least half of women with PCOS already have measurable insulin resistance.

stem: A 32 year old woman presents with complaints of irregular periods over the past 2 years after a long history of regular menses. On physical exam you notice she has some acne present on her face and slightly thinning hair on the top of her head. Her BMI is 29. She tells you she has started having to remove hair on her upper lip frequently. She is "sick of these constant pregnancy scares" and wants something to fix it. You recommend:

options.html: Exercise, diet, and weight loss will be sufficient.

answer:
The correct answer is A. She has two complaints - hirsutism and oligomenorrhea - plus an explicit wish not to conceive. Oral BCPs treat both symptoms and provide the contraception she is asking for, which is why they are the common choice here.

  • Metformin helps oligomenorrhea and may aid fertility - which is not what she wants - and does not address the hirsutism.
  • Clomiphene, a SERM/fertility agent, treats infertility - none of her symptoms.
  • Spironolactone, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, has anti-androgen effects that help hirsutism but not the irregular cycles.
  • E: weight loss may help, but PCOS itself creates a propensity to gain weight, so it may not be sufficient.

stem: You are seeing a new, 33-year old female patient. She tells you that she has always had irregular periods but that this has only recently become a concern as she wishes to conceive. Below is a list of your findings from the history and physical exam. Which of the following options would suggest a cause for her oligomenorrhea?

options.html: Use of spermicide and male condoms

answer:
The correct answer is A. Cushingoid features would point to an adrenal or medication cause at the root of her oligomenorrhea — the best of the listed options.

Note how the distractors are all negative or neutral findings: nipple discharge, if present, would suggest raised prolactin — but its absence tells you little (B). Multiparity (C) actually argues against a problem, since it shows she previously ovulated and conceived. Non-hormonal contraception (D), uterine position (E) and normal body weight (F) should not affect cycles.

stem: Select common features found in patients with PCOS
answer:
The correct answer is E.

All four are on the examination list, so E is right. The lecture groups them by what they are actually showing you, which is more useful than the list itself:

  • Acanthosis nigricans (A), over the back of the neck and in the axilla, usually with skin tags beside it. These are the insulin resistance signs.
  • Hirsutism (B) — terminal hair in a male pattern: face, chin, chest, upper arms.
  • Acne (C) and frontal alopecia (D), which sit with hirsutism as the androgen signs.

One caution the lecture attaches to the same list: rate of onset, ethnicity and parental appearance all have to be weighed before hair growth is called abnormal, and a rapid onset is the androgen-secreting tumour question rather than the PCOS one.

Note this material is taught in the endocrinology block, under the name PMOS, not in reproduction.

stem: Which of these women would NOT be diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome? Select all that apply.

options.html: Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound with no other relevant physical exam or history findings
Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound and hirsutism
Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound and irregular menses for 6 months
Polycystic ovaries on ultrasound, irregular menses for 6 months, and severe acne

answer:
The correct answer is A, D. This year's lecture, 10 - Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS), diagnoses PCOS by a triad, all three needed:

  1. Hyperandrogenism, on exam or on labs
  2. Ovulatory dysfunction: oligomenorrhea or cystic ovaries on ultrasound
  3. Exclusion of other disorders

Cystic ovaries and irregular menses are the same criterion, so neither A (ultrasound alone) nor D (ultrasound plus irregular menses) shows hyperandrogenism. B (hirsutism), C (hirsutism) and E (severe acne) each add it.

stem: When is serum cortisol level greatest?

options.html: Cortisol level is unrelated to time

answer:
The correct answer is A. Cortisol release is pulsatile and follows a diurnal rhythm, rising to a maximum at 8 AM then slowly declining through the day. The 8 AM concentration is usually 2-4x the evening concentration.

Why it matters: an 8 AM serum cortisol is useful to test for adrenal insufficiency - if the daily maximum is too low (<100 nmol/L), you can be confident levels are too low all day. That inference cannot safely be made from a PM measurement.

stem: What would be the best test for diagnosing Cushing's syndrome?
answer:
The correct answer is E. With most endocrine disorders the investigative algorithm is the same: first a test to diagnose the disturbance in the axis, then a test to determine etiology (primary vs. secondary vs. tertiary). If the problem is hormone insufficiency, you stimulate; if the problem is overproduction, you suppress.

Cushing syndrome is a syndrome of excessive glucocorticoid activity, so we need a test showing overproduction of cortisol.

  • A (ACTH stimulation) - tests adrenal responsiveness to exogenous ACTH; an etiology test, used to distinguish primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency.
  • B (dexamethasone suppression test) - tests HPA-axis negative feedback; also an etiology test, the hypercortisolism analogue of the ACTH stimulation test. It is the ideal follow-up once Cushing's is diagnosed.
  • C (8 AM serum cortisol) - most useful for adrenal insufficiency, being cortisol at its maximum.
  • D (PM serum cortisol) - can diagnose Cushing's but is a poor test both analytically (single point measurement at a time of fluctuation) and practically (drawing blood in the evening).
  • E (24-hour urinary free cortisol) - best choice: no blood draw, and a 24-hour integrated measure rather than a point value. Diagnostic if >3x the upper limit of normal.

stem:
A 61-year-old female patient was referred to your clinic from the Cardiology outpatient clinic due to hypokalemic hypertension, for which the cardiologist suspected Primary Hyperaldosteronism. Due to budget cuts by the Ontario government, your hospital is underfunded and you can only perform 1 test. Which of the following tests can be used to diagnose Primary Hyperaldosteronism?

i. Aldosterone/Renin Ratio ii. Furosemide Stimulation test iii. 24-hour urine aldosterone iv. Saline Infusion/Fludrocortisone Suppression Test
answer:
The correct answer is D (i and iv). The cardiologist has already established hypokalemia and hypertension; we are testing for etiology, so per the algorithm in Q31 we need a suppression test for aldosterone.

  • Aldosterone/Renin Ratio works because it reflects both the hormone and its stimulatory signal, which is what lets it separate primary from secondary hyperaldosteronism. An elevated ratio means far more aldosterone is produced than the prevailing renin justifies - i.e. aldosterone elevation is independent of its regulatory signal, equivalent to aldosterone staying up after mineralocorticoid or IV salt loading.
  • Saline infusion / fludrocortisone suppression is a good choice for the same reason any suppression test would be.
  • Furosemide stimulation tests responsiveness to stimulatory signals - used for insufficiency, not this.
  • 24-hour urine aldosterone adds nothing: we already know she is hyperaldosteronemic, and urine aldosterone is a poor diagnostic test in isolation.

See primary aldosteronism and 01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease.

stem: Which of the following descriptions is most likely to be a malignant pheochromocytoma?

options.html: Well-circumscribed, 0.5 cm mass in the adrenal cortex with low density of cells of clear adrenal origin with low nuclear pleomorphism
Well-circumscribed, 0.5 cm mass in the adrenal cortex with high cellularity but normal nuclei and normal mitoses
3 well-circumscribed, 0.5 cm masses, all in the adrenal cortex, with capsular invasion but normal nuclei, low cellularity, and normal mitoses
3 well-circumscribed, 0.5 cm masses, 1 in the adrenal cortex, 1 in the liver, and 1 in the thyroid gland, with vascular invasion, high cellularity and mitotic activity, but normal nuclei
1 poorly-circumscribed (i.e. diffuse growth), 1.5 cm mass in the adrenal medulla with profound nuclear pleomorphism, low cellularity, low mitotic rate, and no vascular or capsular invasion.

answer:
The correct answer is D. The point is the criteria for benign vs. malignant pheochromocytoma, formalised as the PASS criteria - which you are unlikely to be expected to memorise for this course.

The one key feature to remember: the only absolute criterion for malignancy is the presence of distant metastases. D is the only option with distant metastases (liver, thyroid). It is also the only mass fulfilling the PASS criteria (score ≥ 4), if confirmation is needed.

stem:
A 51-year-old woman presents to your general endocrine clinic complaining of generalized weakness, fatigue, nausea, and vomiting over the last two months. Also over that time, she reports a weight loss of 30 pounds. Appetite is unchanged from before, but she mentions that she has been adding increasingly large amounts of salt to all food, as she has been craving salt. She is not on any medications. On physical exam, her blood pressure was measured to be 90/60 sitting, in both arms. Upon standing, she became lightheaded and could not maintain balance.

Her blood work shows the following:

MeasurementValueNormal
Hemoglobin (g/L)156120-160
Na (mmol/L)120135-145
K (mmol/L)6.03.5-5.1
8 AM cortisol (nmol/L)200170-635
8 AM ACTH (pmol/L)1402.2-13.3

Based on this information, what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: A disease in other organ systems

answer:
The correct answer is B. Lab values are not meaningful without clinical context - do not fixate on the numbers; let them complement the clinical picture.

She is clearly showing signs of adrenal insufficiency. Generalized weakness, fatigue and weight loss are non-specific, but salt craving and orthostatic hypotension point strongly to adrenal insufficiency. From history and physical alone the differential could still include anemia from GI bleeding, and dehydration from malnutrition (given nausea/vomiting).

The bloodwork excludes those and reinforces an endocrine cause:

  • Hemoglobin at the upper end of normal - excludes GI bleeding.
  • Hyperkalemic hyponatremia on no medications - indicates dysregulated mineralocorticoid activity.
  • The 8 AM cortisol is "normal" - but this is not normal at all. In a situation this stressful, where her body cannot even maintain her vitals, cortisol should be much higher.
  • What confirms diagnosis and etiology is the ACTH: 10x the reference range while cortisol sits at the low end of normal. That is a failure to respond to the ACTH signal - equivalent to failing an ACTH stimulation test - so the lesion is at the adrenal: primary adrenal insufficiency.

stem: Which of the following is NOT an action of cortisol?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Cortisol is a stress hormone generating three categories of action:

  1. Increases serum glucose and amino acids
  2. Increases lipid and bone catabolism
  3. Increases mineralocorticoid activity

A and B are mineralocorticoid functions. C is correct - hepatic glucose-liberating activity is upregulated. E is correct - lipid catabolism increases, best illustrated by the skin thinning in Cushing syndrome.

D is the exception: increased peripheral glucose uptake would deplete serum glucose. If a person were hypoglycemic, the body needs what little glucose there is to go to vital organs, not peripheral tissues.

stem: A 48-year-old man has recently been diagnosed with pheochromocytoma and has come to you to be evaluated before surgical resection in one week. He does not take any medications. On physical examination, he appears anxious but otherwise well. BMI is 22. Temperature is 37.0°C, heart rate is 112/min, respiration rate is 16/min, and blood pressure is 160/90 mm Hg. Fundoscopic, neurologic, and cardiovascular exams show normal findings. Which of the following would be the next best step in management?

options.html: Hospitalize and give intravenous sodium nitroprusside.

answer:
The correct answer is D. Patients with pheochromocytoma must be pre-treated to stabilize blood pressure before surgery, because both anesthesia and the operation can trigger catecholamine release. The next step is a short-acting alpha-blocker - prazosin, doxazosin or terazosin - targeting a BP of 140/90 to 150/90 mm Hg. Skipping this step can produce a fatal acute hypertensive crisis before or during the operation.

It is critical that beta-blockers are never used before alpha-blockade. Beta-blockade alone leaves unopposed alpha stimulation, giving overwhelming vasoconstriction that can exacerbate or even cause a hypertensive crisis - so C (metoprolol) can be fatal here.

A is wrong for the reason above. B is wrong: even if hydrochlorothiazide lowers BP, it does not address the inappropriate sympathetic activation, and most pheo patients are already vasoconstricted and volume depleted, so a diuretic worsens things. E is wrong: sodium nitroprusside is first-line for acute hypertensive crisis, but this patient is not currently in crisis.

stem: A 41-year-old female presents to your clinic with fatigue, weakness, and lethargy over the last 12 months. She also reports spontaneous, unexplained bruising and weight gain of 40 lbs over the last two months. On physical examination, you notice mild acne, hirsutism, pink striae over the abdomen, moon facies, and a dorsal fat pad. All vital signs were unremarkable. The rest of the physical examination was normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Cushing syndrome is a syndrome of excessive glucocorticoid activity, so look for signs of excess circulating cortisol:

  • Cortisol elevates serum glucose → weight gain from central fat accumulation in a "Cushingoid" distribution (moon facies, dorsal fat pad).
  • Cortisol catabolizes peripheral lipid and protein → skin thinning (digestion of collagen and subcutaneous fat), leaving skin weak and prone to hemorrhage. The likelihood ratio of ecchymoses for Cushing's is 10-11.3. Striae appear from rapid fat expansion plus weakened skin. Muscle weakness develops as muscle is catabolized for amino acids. Osteopenia/osteoporosis follow from osteoblast inhibition plus collagen catabolism.

A (Conn) - no hypokalemic hypertension, so primary aldosteronism does not fit. E - no sympathetic features. D - shares weight gain, fatigue, weakness, lethargy, but the absence of cold intolerance, diminished reflexes, low pulse pressure and bradycardia, plus the presence of steroid-excess signs (acne, hirsutism), makes it unlikely. C - overlaps heavily since hypercortisolism induces insulin resistance, but again the hirsutism and acne favour Cushing's.

stem: A 37-year-old woman presents with a 6 month history of 40 pound weight loss, and a 1 month history of anorexia, recurrent nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, pain, and lightheadedness upon standing. She was diagnosed with Type I diabetes at the age of 9 years; she is currently well-managed with insulin pump therapy. She also was diagnosed with Hashimoto's thyroiditis at age 19; she is currently taking a stable dose of 100 mcg levothyroxine. Family history is significant for hypothyroidism (mother), systemic lupus erythematosus (mother, father), and type I diabetes (brother). Physical examination only reveals orthostatic hypotension and hyperpigmentation of her skin. Which of the following provides the most comprehensive, most likely explanation for her situation?
answer: The correct answer is D. She currently has adrenal insufficiency - orthostatic hypotension plus skin hyperpigmentation (i.e. primary, ACTH-driven) - but in the context of several signs pointing to a global autoimmune condition: she personally has two autoimmune diseases (DM1, Hashimoto's thyroiditis), and her family history is positive for DM1, presumably Hashimoto's, and SLE. The single unifying diagnosis is Polyglandular Autoimmune Syndrome.

flags.title: The syndrome's type label is likely wrong
flags.html: The key, D, is the only unifying diagnosis offered, so it stands as the answer. But type 1 diabetes, Hashimoto's thyroiditis and primary adrenal insufficiency together are classically polyglandular autoimmune syndrome type II (Schmidt), not type I. ⚠ The block's notes do not distinguish the types, so that correction comes from outside them. Flagged, not corrected.

stem: Mutations in which of the following genes is responsible for most (90%) of cases of Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia?
answer:
The correct answer is C. CAH is a disorder of defective adrenal steroid biosynthesis; all genetic causes are autosomal recessive. 21-hydroxylase deficiency accounts for more than 90% of cases - which is why 17-hydroxyprogesterone (the substrate for the 21-hydroxylase reaction) is elevated, and why serum 17-OHP is the standard investigation.

A catalyzes cortisol ↔ cortisone interconversion; does not cause CAH. B can cause CAH but is very rare (and produces an unusual subtype with low androgens and high aldosterone). D converts testosterone → DHT; mutation causes 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, not CAH. E converts testosterone/androstenedione → estrogens; not CAH.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q30-Q45. Tests [[01 - Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease]].
stem: A 3-week-old male infant was found to be homozygous for a mutation in 21-hydroxylase. Which of the following would NOT be expected in his clinical presentation?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Group the features of 21-hydroxylase CAH by hormone abnormality:

  • Substrate buildup: 17-OHP is not consumed, so levels rise → C expected.
  • Cortisol deficiency (precursors need 21-hydroxylase) → hypoglycemia, especially under stress/illness → A expected.
  • Aldosterone deficiency → impaired Na reabsorption, K excretion and H+ excretion → hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis → D and E expected.
  • Androgen excess (excess 17-OHP shunted into androgen synthesis) → in females, virilization (clitoral hypertrophy, labial fusion); in males, inappropriate penile enlargement and scrotal pigmentation.

Because this is a male patient, the expected genital findings are penile enlargement and scrotal pigmentation - not ambiguous genitalia. Hence B is not expected.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q8-Q12. Tests [[03 - Physiologic Changes that Lead to Puberty]], [[04 - Disorders of Puberty]].
stem: Which of the following is correct?

options.html: Testosterone produced by the Leydig cells promotes Wolffian duct development and Mullerian duct regression
Hypothetically, if a developing male fetus lacked MIS production, they would develop a Mullerian duct instead of a Wolffian duct.
A XY patient with complete androgen insensitivity would be phenotypically female both internally and externally.
Dihydrotestosterone induces the development of external male genitalia

answer:
The correct answer is D. DHT does induce differentiation of the male external genitalia.

A is incorrect - testosterone only stimulates Wolffian duct development; MIS is needed to cause Mullerian duct regression. B is incorrect - without MIS the fetus would develop both a Mullerian and a Wolffian duct, since testosterone production is intact. C is incorrect - an XY patient with CAIS (androgen insensitivity syndrome) has a normal external female phenotype but not a normal internal female phenotype, because SRY is still expressed, MIS is still released from Sertoli cells, and the Mullerian ducts still regress.

stem:
A 2-week-old boy with normal-looking genitalia and a hyperpigmented scrotum presents with vomiting and poor feeding. Sodium is 124 mmol/L, potassium 7.1 mmol/L, and glucose 2.8 mmol/L.

Which test confirms the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is A. This is salt-wasting 21-hydroxylase deficiency: cortisol and aldosterone are both lost, giving hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia, with ACTH excess causing hyperpigmentation. The 46,XY infant looks normal and presents in a salt-losing crisis at 1-3 weeks, while the 46,XX infant is caught at birth by ambiguous genitalia. The diagnostic marker is a markedly raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone. T:DHT after hCG is the test for 5-alpha reductase deficiency (C).

I. 24 hour urine for metanephrines, catecholamines and creatinine II. 1 mg dex suppression test, and ACTH III. Serum aldosterone/renin ratio
answer:
The correct answer is D (all of the above). Because the mass is over 1 cm, any zone of the adrenal gland could be involved. All three investigations are therefore needed to rule in/out:

  • a glucocorticoid issue (Addison's / Cushing's) → 1 mg DST + ACTH
  • a mineralocorticoid issue (hyper/hypoaldosteronism) → aldosterone/renin ratio
  • a catecholamine issue (pheochromocytoma) → 24 h urine metanephrines/catecholamines

stem: A male patient with a history of traumatic brain injury presents at your office with anorexia, weight loss, decreased libido, hypoglycemia, constipation, dry skin, low bone mineral density. After ruling out malignancy and reaching a diagnosis, which of the following would not be prescribed?
answer: The correct answer is B. This patient has symptoms of overall hypofunction of the pituitary gland (hypopituitarism), likely secondary to past traumatic brain injury. The key with any hormone deficiency is to replace it, but with a few exceptions. Adrenal insufficiency needs to be replaced with a corticosteroid such as hydrocortisone or prednisone. However, mineralocorticoid replacement is generally only required for primary adrenal insufficiency (such as Addison's disease), and not in this case - in secondary/central disease the aldosterone axis is intact because it is driven by renin-angiotensin, not ACTH. Levothyroxine and testosterone support the thyroid and gonadal axes respectively.

flags.title: Workbook error
flags.html: The key gives the example of mineralocorticoid replacement as "fluticasone". Fluticasone is an inhaled/topical glucocorticoid for asthma and rhinitis, with no mineralocorticoid role at all. The mineralocorticoid used for replacement is fludrocortisone. The letter answer is still B, but for the simpler reason that fluticasone has no place in this patient's regimen.

stem: A 40-year-old female was referred to your endocrine office by her family physician. She was recently diagnosed with hypertension. She complains of enlargement of her jaw, nose, and hands. Her heels from 3 years ago no longer fit her and she reports easier flossing. Which one of the following would not be an appropriate finding or primary treatment option for the presenting case?

options.html: Her serum IGF-1 or fasting GH are elevated
A dose of glucose fails to suppress GH
You prescribe her a somatostatin analogue

answer:
The correct answer is D. GH overproduction in an adult is usually the result of a GH-producing adenoma (acromegaly). Patients typically present with increased acral growth (macrognathia, increased space between teeth, enlargement of nose and frontal bones, enlarged hands and feet), hypertrophic arthropathies of joints, hypertension, cardiomyopathy, increased soft tissue (skin thickening, increased polyps, deeper voice, sleep apnea), hypogonadism, and insulin resistance (thus impaired glucose tolerance). Screening findings include increased IGF-1 (produced by the liver under GH), or a failed glucose suppression test (normally glucose should suppress GH to <1 µg/L).

While somatostatin analogues are a possible treatment for GH-producing adenomas, the first-line treatment is transsphenoidal surgery. Hence D is incorrect.

A somatostatin analogue is a treatment for acromegaly, which is why the question reads "primary treatment": in the lecture it comes after transsphenoidal surgery, not instead of it.

flags.html: The source wrote option C as "a dose of glucose fails to suppress IGF-1". The lecture's confirmatory test is failure of GH to suppress below 1 µg/L on a 75 g OGTT, so C now says GH. As written, C was also a false statement, which gave the question two answers. A reader reported this.

stem: A 6-year-old girl is brought in because her parents are worried due to her slow growth. Records show that she had a normal birth weight and length, and normal growth within the first year of birth. You suspect growth hormone insufficiency. As part of her assessment, you would:

options.html: Perform provocative testing using arginine, clonidine, or glucagon.

answer:
The correct answer is E. The key to this question is that random growth hormone values are NOT useful, due to the pulsatile nature of GH release - hence A and D are incorrect. E is correct because the IGF-1 level is the screening test and provocative testing is diagnostic.

The complete diagnostic criteria for GH deficiency:

  • Short stature - height below 3rd percentile
  • Growth velocity < 25th percentile
  • Bone age delayed by more than 2 SD below chronologic age
  • Inadequate serum GH response to 2 provocative tests (<8 µg/L)

options.html: In girls delayed puberty is defined by no pubertal signs by 13 years of age
Boys are taller than girls because they have an accelerated growth rate during puberty
In early to mid-puberty, LH secretion increased at night
Pulsatile GnRH release is stimulated by Kisspeptin at puberty

answer:
The correct answer is B. B is incorrect - the peak height velocity and total growth during puberty are largely similar between boys and girls. The main reason boys end up taller is that they spend more time growing before the onset of puberty.

A is correct: delayed puberty is defined as the absence or incomplete development of puberty at an age 2.5 SD above the population mean - no pubertal signs by 13 in girls, 14 in boys.

stem: Which of the following is incorrect?

options.html: GABA and neuropeptide Y have an inhibitory effect on the hypothalamus GnHR production in females and males respectively
The first sign of puberty in girls is breast enlargement and penile growth in boys
The effect of estrogen during puberty leads to breast tenderness, mood swings, and vaginal discharge
Delayed puberty is defined as a lack of signs of puberty by 13 in girls, and 14 in boys

answer:
The correct answer is B. GABA and NPY are inhibitory and glutamate is stimulatory. Know the Tanner staging of pubic hair, breast and genital development. The order of pubertal staging:

  • Girls: thelarche → growth spurt → pubarche → menarche
  • Boys: testicular enlargement → penile growth → pubarche → growth

So the first sign in boys is testicular enlargement, not penile growth.

Mnemonic from the key: "Estrogen effects are moody, androgen effects are gross."

stem: A 14-year-old female patient presents in your office. She has breast development and pubic hair but has not started menses. There are no other symptom complaints. She has always been short for her age, although her parents are of reasonable heights. Which of the following is correct?

options.html: Likely constitutional growth delay. Reassure the patient and parents
Order a MRI of head to rule out secondary causes of hypogonadism
Order a karyotype to rule out Turner's syndrome

answer: The correct answer is C. Although constitutional growth delay and secondary hypogonadism are both possible causes of delayed puberty, the most appropriate action is to rule in/out Turner syndrome, which presents with short stature and primary hypogonadism. The patient fits the picture: Turner syndrome patients usually have pubarche, and about 10-15% have breast development as well.

stem: An 8-year-old boy is brought in. He recently developed strong body odour, grew pubic hair and rapid growth in height and weight in the last 6 months. On physical examination his height and weight are at >95% percentiles, bilaterally enlarged testes. Pubic hair T3, penis T5. Which of the following would NOT be consistent or appropriate with this presentation?
answer: The correct answer is B. First determine whether this is a central (gonadotropin-dependent) or peripheral cause of precocious puberty. Because the patient has bilateral testicular enlargement, it is unlikely that the testes are an autonomous source of testosterone - bilateral enlargement means they are being driven by gonadotropins. This is therefore gonadotropin-dependent precocious puberty, so serum LH/FSH would be elevated, not below normal. Treatment is a continuous LHRH analogue, which suppresses pubertal development.

stem: What is the expected phenotype of a patient who is 46XY but has a complete defect in the androgen receptor?

options.html: Completely female external and internal genitalia, with normal female puberty and menses
Completely female external and internal genitalia, with no menses but otherwise normal female puberty
Completely female external genitalia, both testes and ovaries, and no menses but otherwise normal puberty
Ambiguous external genitalia, female internal genitalia, and normal female puberty
Completely female external genitalia, only testes internally, and absent menses but otherwise normal female puberty.

answer:
The correct answer is E. This is Complete Androgen Insensitivity.

Internally there will be testes only. Recall that creation of the internal genitalia is sex steroid-independent: testes form under the influence of SRY, and Sertoli cells then generate Mullerian Inhibiting Substance (MIS), which prevents development of the ovaries, fallopian tubes and upper ⅓ of the vagina.

Externally, the lack of androgen signalling at the receptor produces female external genitalia, and at puberty female secondary sex characteristics develop. But because the female internal genitalia are absent, menses does not occur.

See 09 - Disorders of Sexual Differentiation.

stem:
A 45-year-old man with a history of primary adrenal insufficiency due to autoimmune Addison’s disease presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe fatigue, dizziness, and vomiting. He reports a recent gastroenteritis with poor oral intake. On examination:

  • Blood pressure: 85/50 mmHg
  • Heart rate: 120 bpm
  • Temperature: 38.3°C
  • Skin: diffuse hyperpigmentation
  • Mucous membranes: dry
  • Patient appears confused and lethargic

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?

options.html: Wait for cortisol and ACTH results before starting any treatment.
Give IV fluids only, then monitor vital signs and urine output closely.
IV hydrocortisone now, aggressive dextrose-saline fluids, and correct electrolytes.
Give oral fludrocortisone and schedule endocrine follow-up in 1 week.
Start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics only, as hypotension is likely septic shock.

answer: The correct answer is C. From the deck's next slide (adrenal crisis): the trigger is a stressor (infection, surgery, trauma) in known adrenal insufficiency; features are refractory hypotension, shock, GI symptoms, altered mental status and hyperpigmentation; labs show hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia. Immediate management: 1. IV hydrocortisone · 2. aggressive IV fluids, 0.9% saline + dextrose · 3. correct electrolytes · 4. treat the trigger. The lecture is the same, and explicit that you do not wait for results (A).

stem:
A 54-year old female presents with a 3-week history of progressive weakness, nausea, and vomiting. She has lost approximately 15 pounds. She is on no medications. Although she is alert, she is slow to respond to your questions. Her blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg and heart rate 115 bpm when lying and on standing, her blood pressure is 70/40 mmHg with a heart rate of 150 bpm. She is afebrile. Her weight is 50 kg and BMI of 23. She has hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa.

What are the initial steps in her management – select up to 4 as points are deducted if more than 4 are chosen.
answer:
The correct answers are A, C, F and G. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease.

From the review session. Orthostatic shock with buccal hyperpigmentation points to primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's). ACTH runs very high, and POMC, the precursor it is cut from, also yields melanocyte-stimulating hormone, which darkens the buccal mucosa. Resuscitate with IV fluids, check electrolytes and glucose, draw ACTH and cortisol straight away, then give high-dose hydrocortisone without waiting for the results. A 24-hour urine cortisol (H) has no role: it takes too long while she may become unstable, and it is a test for cortisol excess, not deficiency.

Weight loss, vomiting, marked orthostatic hypotension and buccal hyperpigmentation are primary adrenal insufficiency heading into crisis. Resuscitate with IV normal saline, and draw the bloods that answer the immediate questions: electrolytes and creatinine (Na↓, K↑, azotemia), glucose (hypoglycemia), and a paired cortisol and ACTH before steroids are given, without waiting for the results to treat. Dextrose (B) is added if she is hypoglycemic; calcium, thyroid tests and a 24-h urine cortisol (D, E, H) do not change the first hour.

stem:
For each scenario below, choose the single BEST screening test:

i. A 31 year-old female has a 3-month history of proximal muscle weakness, worsening diabetes, easy bruising, and hirsutism. Her only medication is the oral contraceptive.

options.html: 24 hour urine for catecholamines and metanephrines

answer:
The correct answer is D. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease.

From the review session. The room split between A, D and E, and the presenter keyed D. Estrogen in the oral contraceptive raises hepatic cortisol-binding globulin, so total serum cortisol reads falsely high. That spoils the morning cortisol after 1 mg dexamethasone (E) and a plain AM cortisol (A), while the 24-hour urine measures only free cortisol and is unaffected. ⭐ Look in the stem for a drug that raises CBG; if there is one, pick the 24-hour urine. Without one, the presenter opens with both the 24-hour urine and the 1 mg DST, because Cushing's needs more than one positive test and a high pretest probability. Late-night salivary cortisol is the third test, but most community labs cannot run it. An AM cortisol on its own is mainly a test for adrenal insufficiency: a low value tells you something, a high one does not.

Proximal weakness and easy bruising are the highest-likelihood-ratio Cushing signs, so screen for cortisol excess. Of the screens, the lecture says the 1 mg DST is not useful in women on an estrogen-containing oral contraceptive (estrogen raises cortisol-binding globulin, so total cortisol looks unsuppressed), which leaves the 24-hour urine free cortisol. A single AM cortisol (A) cannot diagnose excess, and ACTH (B) comes after cortisol excess is proven.

From the review session. Episodic pallor, anxiety and hypertension suggest pheochromocytoma. Ask for the metanephrines, not only the catecholamines: they are produced continuously within the tumour, which makes them the most sensitive screen.

Episodic spells with hypertension suggest pheochromocytoma, screened biochemically by metanephrines. The lecture's best single test is plasma free metanephrines (99% sensitive), which is not offered; urinary fractionated metanephrines are next (97%). Urine VMA (G) is only 64% sensitive, and imaging (I) comes after the biochemistry.

stem:
A 19-year-old previously healthy man is brought to the emergency department with a history of a mild pharyngitis and then a high fever over the past 24 hours. In the emergency room, he is confused, hard to arouse, and has extensive areas of purpura. Vital signs include temperature 39°C, pulse rate 102/minute, respiratory rate 21/minute, and blood pressure 80/55 mm Hg. Lab studies show a serum sodium of 115 mM, potassium 5.3 mM, chloride 92 mM, CO2 22 mM, glucose 3.2 mM, and serum creatinine 156 uM.

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is B. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease.

From the review session. The cause is meningococcemia (pharyngitis, fever, purpura), which can bleed into both adrenals: Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome, giving shock with low sodium, high potassium and low glucose. A student asked about thyroid storm, since fever, pharyngitis and tachycardia fit it too. The labs separate them, because storm does not cause hyponatremia, hyperkalemia or hypoglycemia. So does the presentation: a storm patient is agitated or combative, tremulous and warm, not obtunded on arrival. His confusion can come from the hypoglycemia and the shock.

Fever, purpura and shock after a pharyngitis suggest meningococcal sepsis, and adrenal haemorrhage is one of the lecture's causes of primary insufficiency. The labs are the primary pattern: hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia and azotemia, because the whole cortex is lost, aldosterone as well as cortisol. TB (A) is a cause of Addison's, but not over 24 hours.

He is no medications but has a 45 pack year history of cigarette smoking. On physical exam his blood pressure is 165/110 mm Hg. He is overweight with a BMI of 28. A radiograph of the spine reveals a compression fracture at T10. Lab findings include a random plasma glucose 18.5 mM, serum sodium 134 mM, and serum potassium 2.9 mM.

I) Which one of the following test results would be most likely in this man?

options.html: An 8:00 AM serum cortisol of 45.9 nM after 1 mg dexamethasone PO the night before (Nl <50 nmol/L)
A 24 hour urine free cortisol level of 439 nmol/d (normal 120 – 384 nmol/d)
An AM plasma ACTH level 232 pM (normal < 14 pM)
A 1.3 cm pituitary mass consistent with an adenoma on an MRI

answer:
The correct answer is B. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease.

From the review session. The fragility fracture, hypertension, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia and proximal myopathy all point to Cushing's, so expect a raised urine free cortisol.

Proximal weakness, a vertebral fracture, hypertension, hyperglycemia and hypokalemia add up to cortisol excess, and the high-LR signs (fracture, proximal weakness) are present. A raised 24-h urine free cortisol fits. A post-dexamethasone cortisol of 45.9 is suppressed, i.e. normal (A); an A1c of 6.0% does not fit a random glucose of 18.5 (E).

stem:
A 36-year-old woman with Addison's disease takes hydrocortisone 15 mg in the morning and 5 mg in the afternoon, with fludrocortisone. She phones with influenza and a fever of 38.6°C. She is eating and drinking and has not vomited.

What should she do?

options.html: Triple her hydrocortisone for three days
Double her dose for one day only
Stop the fludrocortisone until she recovers
Go to the emergency department for IV hydrocortisone

answer: The correct answer is B. The lecture's rule of 3s: with flu and similar illness, increase the dose 3-fold for 3 days. She needs an injection or IV hydrocortisone (E) only if she cannot take or absorb oral doses, e.g. vomiting or severe diarrhoea. Failing to stress-dose is how chronic insufficiency becomes an adrenal crisis.

stem:
A patient has a low 8 AM cortisol and symptoms of adrenal insufficiency.

Which finding points to primary rather than secondary adrenal insufficiency?
answer: The correct answer is C. Primary insufficiency destroys the whole cortex, so aldosterone is lost as well as cortisol: potassium rises, ACTH is high (hence hyperpigmentation), and fludrocortisone is needed. In secondary insufficiency the aldosterone axis is preserved and K⁺ is normal. Hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, fatigue and hypotension (A, B, D, E) occur in both.

stem:
A 48-year-old man has experienced constant back pain exacerbated by movement over the past month. He also reports increasing difficulty climbing stairs over the past 4 months. He is no medications but has a 45 pack year history of cigarette smoking. On physical exam his blood pressure is 165/110 mm Hg. He is overweight with a BMI of 28. A radiograph of the spine reveals a compression fracture at T10. Lab findings include a random plasma glucose 18.5 mM, serum sodium 134 mM, and serum potassium 2.9 mM.

II) Based on the information you have to this point, which of the following pathologic lesions is most likely to explain his findings?
answer:
The correct answer, as keyed by the deck, is C. No written rationale. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Adrenal Gland Disease.

From the review session. Common things being common: an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma causes about 70% of endogenous Cushing's. Several students picked adrenocortical carcinoma (A) for the short history and the spinal fracture. It would suppress ACTH, and the fracture is osteoporotic from cortisol excess, which can happen at any vertebral level, not a metastasis from the adrenal. Small cell lung cancer (B) fits the smoking history, but ectopic ACTH is rare. Pheochromocytoma (D) gives adrenaline-type symptoms instead. Students also read the hypertension and low potassium as aldosterone excess. ⭐ Cortisol at very high levels acts on the mineralocorticoid receptor itself, so any cause of hypercortisolism gives both, with or without aldosterone.

Once exogenous steroid is excluded (he takes no medications), the commonest cause of endogenous Cushing's is an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease), and the review session confirmed that is the logic behind "the information you have to this point". The lecture separates the causes by ACTH (dependent: pituitary, ectopic ACTH or CRH; independent: adrenal adenoma, hyperplasia, carcinoma), then localises.

flags.title: Small cell lung cancer is a strong alternative
flags.html: A 45 pack-year smoker with a fast course, marked hypokalemia (2.9) and hypertension is the classic picture of ectopic ACTH from small cell lung cancer (B). The lecture lists ectopic ACTH as an ACTH-dependent cause and says its ACTH is "usually higher", but does not give hypokalemia or smoking as discriminators. The deck keys C.

stem:
A 55-year-old man with a known non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma has fatigue and cold intolerance. His TSH is 3.1 mIU/L (normal 0.3-4.2) and his free T4 is low.

How should these results be interpreted?

options.html: Euthyroid, because the TSH is within the normal range
Primary hypothyroidism, needing a repeat TSH in about six weeks
Assay interference; repeat only the TSH
Central hypothyroidism; the TSH is inappropriately normal

answer: The correct answer is E. TSH is an excellent screen for primary disease and unreliable in secondary. With a pituitary lesion, a normal TSH beside a low free T4 is "inappropriately normal" and is the diagnosis of central hypothyroidism. Replace on the free T4, never the TSH, and treat any adrenal insufficiency before starting thyroxine. Primary hypothyroidism would have a high TSH (B).

stem:
A 29-year-old primigravida who received no prenatal care had marked vaginal bleeding after the onset of labor at 38 weeks gestation. Cesarean section was done and a lacerated low-lying placenta was removed. She remained hypotensive for 6 hours and required transfusion of 12 packed RBC units. She was discharged home but was not able to breast-feed. Over the next 2 months, she also noted increasing fatigue, anorexia, and lightheadness especially when she stands up. Despite not breastfeeding, her periods have not resumed.

Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her current symptoms?
answer:
The correct answer is B. No written rationale in the deck. The presenter's reasoning from the review session comes first; the paragraph after it is ours, checked against Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease.

From the review session. Postpartum hemorrhage and hypotension infarct the pituitary, which is enlarged in pregnancy: no lactation (prolactin), no menses (LH and FSH), fatigue and orthostasis (ACTH). A student asked about treatment. She is acutely unwell, so replace what is missing, hydrocortisone first, then levothyroxine if she has central hypothyroidism. Lactation cannot be restored, and most patients do not recover gonadal function, so they need long-term estrogen and progesterone, which also affects future pregnancies.

Postpartum haemorrhage with prolonged hypotension, then failure of lactation (prolactin), amenorrhoea (gonadotropins) and orthostatic fatigue (ACTH), is several anterior pituitary axes failing together: pituitary infarction after postpartum haemorrhage (Sheehan syndrome). Infarction is one of the lecture's causes of hypopituitarism. Adrenal haemorrhage (A) would not stop lactation or menses.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. Normal growth velocity with a delayed bone age, late puberty and a family history of late puberty is constitutional delay, a normal variant with a normal adult height, so reassurance is the treatment. In familial short stature the bone age matches chronological age and puberty is on time (A). GH deficiency and hypothyroidism slow the growth velocity (B, C).

stem: Is an estrogen block required for female-to-male transition?

options.html: Yes, so that the effects of testosterone is not counteracted
Yes, so that the feminizing effects of estrogen is downregulated
No, because testosterone will automatically downregulate estrogen
No, because the effects of testosterone supercedes the effect of estrogen

answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 08 - Introduction to Transgender Medicine and 09 - Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Gonadal Axis. Gender-affirming hormones have two goals: suppress the endogenous hormone and replace as for a hypogonadal patient. The regimens are asymmetric:

  • Trans women need an anti-androgen (spironolactone, cyproterone acetate) or a GnRH agonist alongside estrogen.
  • Trans men are listed with exogenous testosterone alone, because testosterone suppresses the ovary itself. At therapeutic levels (target 14-24 nmol/L) it exerts negative feedback on the HPG axis, ↓ LH/FSH, and so ↓ ovarian estradiol.
  • A, B fail because a separate estrogen block is unnecessary: the suppression comes free with the testosterone.
  • D reaches the right "no" for the wrong reason. Testosterone does not overpower circulating estrogen at the receptor; it removes the estrogen upstream by shutting down gonadotropins.

stem: Correctly order the following pubertal milestones for girls from earliest to latest onset:
answer:
The correct answer is C, A, D, B.

From 04 - Disorders of Puberty. The lecture gives the girls' sequence as thelarche → growth spurt → pubarche → menarche:

  • Thelarche (C) is the first sign in most girls, at about 10.3 years. Ovarian estradiol drives breast development.
  • The growth spurt (A) comes early in girls, at Tanner 2-3 (in boys it comes later, at Tanner 3-4, which is why boys finish taller).
  • Pubarche (D) follows.
  • Menarche (B) comes last, at about 12.7 years, roughly 2.5 years after thelarche.

Two traps:

  • 15% of girls have pubarche first, because it is adrenal rather than gonadal, so the order is typical, not invariant.
  • Menarche is never early in the sequence: it needs enough estradiol and progesterone to build and shed endometrium, which comes after peak height velocity.

stem: Which of the following is NOT an accepted definition of delayed puberty?

options.html: Absence of puberty >13 years old for females
Absence of puberty >15 years old for males
Absence of puberty > 2.5 SD of the average age for either sex
Incomplete puberty > 2.5 SD of the average age for either sex

answer:
The correct answer is B. The standard definition for males is >14 years old.

From 04 - Disorders of Puberty. Delayed puberty is defined statistically as the absence or incomplete development of puberty at an age 2.5 SD above the population mean. That works out to 13 years for girls and 14 years for boys. So B's 15-year cut-off is not the accepted definition, and waiting until 15 would delay the workup (karyotype, LH/FSH, bone age) by a year. The other three are accepted:

  • A matches the girls' cut-off of 13.
  • C (absent puberty at >2.5 SD) is the definition itself.
  • D is also accepted, because the definition covers incomplete puberty as well as absent puberty. Arrested puberty counts.

options.html: Peripheral, from androgen outside the testes

Bilaterally enlarged testes (≥ 4 mL) mean central; virilisation with small testes (< 3 mL) and low LH mean peripheral, with androgen coming from elsewhere (CAH, an adrenal tumour, exogenous testosterone). stem: Which of the following best describes polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS)?

options.html: A diagnosis of PCOS can be made entirely based on evidence of cystic ovaries on ultrasound.
PCOS can be diagnosed entirely based on history and physical examination.
PCOS is rare compared to other endocrinopathies.
Excess estradiol is a common finding in PCOS.

answer:
The correct answer is B. PCOS is a symptom complex with multiple definitions; a commonly used one requires 2 of 3:

  • Presence of cysts on ovarian imaging
  • Evidence of androgen excess (e.g. acne, hirsutism)
  • Disrupted menstruation (amenorrhea)

Since both androgen excess and disrupted menstruation can be established from history and physical exam alone, B can be correct. A is wrong - cystic ovaries are extremely common and never sufficient alone under any definition. C is wrong - PCOS is common. D is wrong - excess androgens and estrone are found in PCOS; estradiol levels are usually normal.

stem: Which of the following does NOT increase serum cortisol levels?

options.html: Intense or prolonged physical exertion immediately prior to test

answer:
The correct answer is C. Anything affecting either the total amount of cortisol or the amount of cortisol-binding globulin (CBG) can interfere with a serum cortisol measurement.

  • A does interfere - intense or prolonged exertion induces cortisol release.
  • B does - cortisol antagonizes insulin and raises serum glucose, so in hypoglycemia cortisol rises.
  • D and E do - pregnancy and OCP use elevate CBG, and to maintain free cortisol the body synthesizes more, raising the total concentration.
  • C does not: it is unreasonable to release cortisol and raise glucose when glucose is already high.

stem: Which of the following is INCORRECT regarding pheochromocytomas?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Built around the lecture's "Rule of 10s":

  • ~10% arise in association with familial syndromes (MEN2A, MEN2B, VHL, NF1, NF2)
  • ~10% are extra-adrenal
  • ~10% are bilateral
  • ~10% are malignant ← so ~90% are benign, making C the incorrect statement
  • ~10% arise in childhood

The key also walks through reasoning it out if you forget which items the 10% attaches to: tumours are generally rare in children and almost never environmental when they do occur, so "10% childhood" and "10% familial" support each other and are unlikely to be the wrong one. "10% bilateral" is reasonable because it implies 90% unilateral, far more plausible than the inverse - bilateral disease would require either two independent de novo neoplastic events or undetected metastasis to the other gland.

stem: Which of the following structures gives rise to the female external genitalia?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Urogenital sinus.

From Development of the Female Reproductive System. C wins by elimination: it is the only option that is not an internal duct. Female external genitalia develop in weeks 9-14, driven by estrogen and the absence of DHT, from the swellings around the urogenital sinus's opening: genital tubercle → clitoris, urethral folds → labia minora, labioscrotal swellings → labia majora, all three staying unfused. The sinus itself gives the lower 2/3 of the vagina via the sinovaginal bulbs.

  • A fails: the paramesonephric (Müllerian) ducts form the tubes, uterus, cervix and upper 1/3 of the vagina - all internal.
  • B, D fail: one structure under two names (mesonephric = Wolffian), which degenerates without testosterone and leaves only remnants such as Gartner's duct.
